title: Application of python image analysis tools for particle structure detachment detection in high‑speed videos during model filter regeneration
author: Desens, Meyer, et al.

steps.title: Detect particle detachments in video
steps.instruction: Run the Tkinter GUI (module 1.1) to select a video file and an output directory (1.2). The program extracts the first frame, displays it, and lets the user click four corner points that define the filter channel boundaries (1.3); the points are reordered with the order_points function. A perspective‑transform matrix is computed to warp every subsequent frame into a top‑down view of the channel (physical size 120 mm × 3 mm) and scaling factors (mm per pixel) are set. After confirming ROI and calibration (1.4), the analysis starts in a separate processing thread. Each frame is transformed to isolate the ROI; optional frame‑skip can be applied to analyse only selected frames. Background subtraction uses OpenCV MOG2 (1.5) with a history of 1000 frames and a learning rate of 0.1 (10 % weighting per frame) (1.7). Morphological opening (kernel = 3 × 3, iterations = 2) and closing (iterations = 1) remove noise. Contours are found with cv2.findContours; only those larger than a user‑defined size (e.g., 20 px) and with aspect‑ratio ≥ 1:4 (1.8, 1.9) are kept. For each new contour the script saves four reference images (previous frame, current frame, contour overlay, filled‑mask) into a particle subfolder (1.10). Contour area is computed in pixels and converted to real‑world units using the scale factors. Results are logged continuously in a pandas DataFrame and periodically written to a temporary .CSV file. When all frames are processed, the final dataset is exported as an Excel file and temporary files are consolidated or removed (1.12). The user reviews the list and images and may discard or reclassify any incorrect detections.

substeps.instruction: Launch GUI and select video and output folder.
Extract first frame and define ROI by clicking four corners.
Reorder points, compute perspective transform, set physical dimensions (120 mm × 3 mm) and scaling factors.
Start main analysis thread; apply optional frame skip.
Perform MOG2 background subtraction (history = 1000 frames, learning rate = 0.1).
Apply morphological opening (3 × 3, 2 iterations) and closing (1 iteration).
Find contours larger than 20 px and aspect‑ratio ≥ 1:4.
Save previous frame, current frame, overlay, and mask images for each contour.
Log contour area, convert to real units, write interim CSV, then export final Excel file.

steps.title: Verify detected detachments
steps.instruction: For each particle folder, the second script reads the marked image file (2.3) that shows the candidate detachment in red. An HSV‑based mask isolates the red contour and a bounding box around it is computed (2.7). Both the previous and current frames are cropped to this bounding box with a small user‑defined margin (2.8‑2.10). The cropped images are binarized with THRESH_BINARY_INV (2.12), turning darker particle structures white and lighter background black. An absolute difference image of the two binary frames is created (2.14) and a morphological opening (kernel = 3 × 3, iterations = 1) is applied to reduce noise (2.15). If the white‑pixel area in the difference image exceeds 20 px, the detachment is labeled correct (probability = 1) (2.19); otherwise it is labeled incorrect (probability = 0) (2.18). The 20 px threshold corresponds to an area‑equivalent diameter of roughly 100 µm. Debug images—cropped region (2.9, 2.11), binary threshold (2.13), and difference mask (2.20)—are saved in a subfolder of each particle directory. Finally, all probabilities (0 or 1) and the measured difference area in pixels are compiled into an Excel file (2.21, 2.22).

substeps.instruction: Load marked image and isolate red contour via HSV masking.
Compute bounding box around contour and add user‑defined margin.
Crop previous and current frames to the bounding box.
Create absolute difference image and apply opening (3 × 3, 1 iteration).
If white‑pixel area > 20 px, set probability = 1; else probability = 0.
Save debug images (cropped region, binary mask, difference mask).
Write probabilities and difference areas to an Excel summary.

description: The approach is implemented across two integrated modules, built on OpenCV [15,16], and NumPy [17], to automatically identify particle structure detachments. The first module detects candidate detachment events by analyzing the entire video frame by frame and the second step is for verifying the candidate detachment events detected in the first module. A representative test was conducted using a model filter channel loaded with carbon black, where a quartz glass window was integrated into the channel wall to allow perpendicular high‑speed imaging. Once the carbon black layer began visibly breaking up, a CP90‑25P‑M72 camera (Optronis GmbH) recorded 796,000 frames at 1000 fps under 150 W LED panel illumination (GSVitec MultiLed G8). The camera, equipped with a Zeiss Macro lens (Milvus 2/100 M), captured images at 5120 × 200 px with a 1/10,000 s exposure time.
